title: Theoretical Framework: Epistemic Systems Theory

Chapter 3
Theoretical Framework: Epistemic Systems
Theory
Chapter abstract. This chapter introduces Epistemic Systems Theory and its four
propositions: structural determination, thermodynamic constraint, psychometric ac-
countability, and participation and evidence-based production.
It formalises repu-
tation update, an epistemic Hamiltonian, source entropy, heat capacity, and a BRS
measurement model, and it explains each formal object in plain language. It distin-
guishes formal analogies from empirical laws and states the conditions under which
each proposition would be rejected.
Epistemic Systems Theory (EST) treats a social media radio platform as
a socio-technical epistemic system: a coupled structure of platform architecture,
cognitive states, and social trust networks whose proposed epistemic outputs (the
diversity of information that reaches users, the distribution of credibility, the rate
of misinformation propagation) are hypothesised to depend substantially on archi-
tecture. The relative size of architectural and user contributions is an empirical
question, not an assumption veried by the present survey. EST is developed here
as the unifying lens of the thesis. It rests on four propositions: EST-P1 (struc-
tural determination), EST-P2 (thermodynamic constraint), EST-P3 (psychometric
35

CHAPTER 3. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK: EPISTEMIC SYSTEMS THEORY 36
accountability), and EST-P4 (participation and evidence-based production). From
these propositions the hypotheses of Chapter 1 are deduced.

3.1
Why a New Framework Is Needed
The review motivates an original synthesis of three concerns: how platform rules
shape exposure, how audiences evaluate sources and messages, and how consequen-
tial metrics are measured. EST connects these concerns through four propositions
and a platform specication. Dierences among the reviewed studies reect dier-
ences in design and context as well as possible theoretical disagreement; they do not
establish that all existing approaches are incompatible. The contribution of EST
is its proposed integration and testable commitments, rather than an assertion of
universal explanatory superiority.
EST uses mathematical structures from information theory and network

CHAPTER 3. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK: EPISTEMIC SYSTEMS THEORY 37
modelling to make its proposals explicit. Shannon's (1948) entropy provides a mea-
sure of a specied probability distribution, and DeGroot's (1974) model species a
class of opinion updates. The Hamiltonian and free-energy terms below are author-
dened social-system analogies. A shared notation alone does not transfer a physical
law, an equilibrium, or a stability theorem to a platform: those conclusions require
the actual update equations and their assumptions. Appendix E states the limited
mathematical results that follow under explicit conditions. EST does not claim that
social networks obey physical thermodynamic laws.
3.2
EST-P1: Structural Determination
3.2.1
Statement
The epistemic properties of a platform, the distribution of credibility, the diver-
sity of information reaching users, and the rate of misinformation propagation, are
primarily determined by the platform's architectural design: its incentive struc-
tures, trust-propagation algorithms, credibility metrics, and content-ranking func-
tions. Architecture is the primary independent variable in epistemic governance,
not a neutral substrate for user behaviour.
3.2.2
Formal Grounding
Let a social media radio platform be modelled as a tuple
P = (U, C, A, R, G),
(3.1)

CHAPTER 3. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK: EPISTEMIC SYSTEMS THEORY 38
where U is the user set, C the content set, A the recommendation algorithm, R the
reputation function, and G the governance rules. EST-P1 asserts that the epistemic
outcome function
Ω(P, t) = f(A, R, G) + g(U, C, t)
(3.2)
In plain terms. The equation says that what a listener can know is limited by the
platform's exposure rule. Change what the architecture shows, and you change the set
of evaluations that are possible; you do not automatically change what is true.
In ordinary terms: this working decomposition separates a platform-rule
contribution from a user-and-content contribution. It does not measure their relative
importance. An additive split omits possible interactions, and adding a constant
to f while subtracting it from g leaves the outcome unchanged. The dominance
comparison therefore requires an identied decomposition, a common scale, reference
conditions, and a dened domain before testing.
is dominated by the architectural triple (A, R, G): ∥f∥∞≫∥g∥∞under typ-
ical operating conditions. This inequality is a theoretical dominance hypothesis, not
an estimate from the eld survey. It requires a dened outcome scale and compar-
isons that separately identify architectural and user contributions. The literature in
Chapter 2 motivates studying network diusion and exposure without identifying
this inequality. Vosoughi et al. (2018) compare news cascades; Bail et al. (2018)
examine an intervention exposing participants to opposing political views. Neither
separates the functions f and g or establishes architectural dominance in audio
communication. The feed experiment of Gauthier et al. (2026) supplies more direct

CHAPTER 3. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK: EPISTEMIC SYSTEMS THEORY 39
evidence about a specic ranking intervention, but its outcome-specic ndings also
show why the scope of P1 must be stated explicitly.
3.2.3
Architectural Implications
EST-P1 motivates three design commitments, not empirically established necessi-
ties. Credibility requires auditable inputs: the reference BRS should document
broadcast consistency, retention, source use, corrections, and endorsement rather
than equating popularity with credibility. Retention and source diversity are not
themselves tests of factual accuracy. Recommendation requires explicit ob-
jectives: quality and diversity constraints should be stated alongside engagement
targets so that their trade-os can be evaluated rather than assumed benecial.
Governance requires accountable rules: proposed down-weighting and moder-
ation should be inspectable, contestable, and proportionate to the uncertainty of the
detection system (Chapter 4). These are operational proposals whose consequences
remain open to empirical testing.
3.2.4
A Reputation Update with Structural Guarantees
The structural claim of EST-P1 becomes testable only when the reputation update
is given a precise form. The BRS of broadcaster u is designed as a modied DeGroot
(1974) consensus process in which the update at session t is driven partly by peer
endorsement and partly by objective broadcast evidence:

evidence anchor. The cap stops one highly reputed node from dominating. In plain

In ordinary terms: the next reputation score blends the scores of endors-
ing peers with a separate evidence signal. If λ = .2, the update allocates 20% of
its weight to that signal and 80% to peer-weighted reputation. This is an illustra-
tive setting, not an estimated eld parameter. Stable scores can still be wrong if
endorsements or the anchor are inaccurate.
where Auv is a nonnegative endorsement weight and each row of A sums to
one. Negative endorsements must be handled separately rather than included in a
matrix described as row-stochastic. The input Xu(t) is a specied evidence signal;
calling it evidence does not establish its accuracy.
For xed A and a xed input vector X, the full update contracts in the supre-
mum norm by at most 1−λ, and has the unique xed point B∗= λ[I−(1−λ)A]−1X.
The unanchored row-stochastic component alone is non-expansive, not necessarily
strictly contractive. Time-varying inputs need additional conditions for convergence,
and a constant anchor can still produce consensus. Thus the mathematical result
describes stability under stated assumptions, not truth or resistance to manipula-
tion.

evidence of observed diusion in the eld sample.

An episode, an extract, and a repost may carry dierent context. A defensi-
ble propagation record would preserve content identiers, parent-post links, version
changes, and event times. Exposure is not automatically completed listening, and
resharing is not necessarily agreement, consistent with the sharingjudgment dis-

The appropriate formal object is a time-indexed event graph. Links connect
earlier to later events. Repeated appearances of a participant are separate events; an
actor-level feedback cycle becomes a time-ordered sequence when expanded. Trans-
mission probabilities would require observed opportunities to share as denominators,

not just successful repost counts. None is estimated from the 52 questionnaires.
The schematic distinguishes a ranking change that alters exposure from a
prompt that alters resharing after exposure. Measuring only PB cannot identify
all these paths. The drawings specify what to observe; they do not supply missing
observations or a tted network model.
3.4
EST-P2: Thermodynamic Constraint
3.4.1
Statement
EST-P2 proposes that diversity and reputation concentration depend on the net-
work, its update rules, and the objectives governing exposure. Some engagement-
oriented congurations may concentrate attention, while diversity constraints may
change their performance. These are conditional predictions, not a physical law
requiring every network to lose diversity or every quality improvement to reduce
engagement. User preferences, new sources, and the content supply can also change
the outcome. The thermodynamic vocabulary species an analogy to be evaluated
rather than a reason to exclude these alternative processes.

disturbed by new content. High capacity means slower, steadier updating.

must be assessed independently of exposure frequency. Undened capacities, includ-

by arbitrary constants. Active days, session counts, and the time window also need
to be xed before comparing this index across broadcasters. It is a score-volatility
index, not measured physical heat capacity.
3.4.4
Implications
EST-P2 proposes two conditional predictions. Under the model's specied reinforce-
ment rules, an architecture without a diversity counterforce is expected to concen-
trate attention and reputation. Under the specied ranking objective, imposing di-
versity and quality constraints is expected to reduce raw engagement relative to G0.
Neither prediction follows from a physical conservation law: novelty, better match-
ing, or dierent user preferences could allow diversity and engagement to increase
together. Such a nding would challenge the claimed trade-o within the relevant
scope, rather than constitute a thermodynamic impossibility. The simulated trade-
o index in Chapter 6 describes the selected model and scaling convention; it is not
an empirical universal constant.
3.5
EST-P3: Psychometric Accountability
3.5.1
Statement
Consequential metrics must meet psychometric standards commensurate with their
consequence. A metric that governs access, visibility, or reputation on an epistemic
platform is a credential: it changes what users can do and what they believe, and it

CHAPTER 3. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK: EPISTEMIC SYSTEMS THEORY 47
must be validated as a measurement instrument. This proposition applies the Stan-
dards for Educational and Psychological Testing (American Educational Research
Association et al., 2014) to platform metrics. It has two design consequences. First,
the BRS must have an explicit measurement model, quantiable reliability, and a re-
ported condence interval rather than a point score. Second, the survey instruments
used to evaluate the platform must be calibrated on measured data with reported
item statistics, reliability coecients, and, where the sample permits, conrmatory
factor analysis.
EST-P3 also governs the fairness of consequential metrics: a score that re-
wards accumulated history systematically disadvantages new broadcasters, so the
BRS includes career-phase weighting and a Matthew-eect cap (Chapter 4). Con-
vergent self-report evidence, such as the star-rating association, addresses only one
part of a validity argument. Consequences, fairness, and accuracy require evidence
beyond agreement between audience ratings.
3.5.2
The Explicit Measurement Model
The proposed model for the 11-item broadcaster-rating questionnaire has three cor-
related factors: Broadcast Rigor, Social Validation, and Information Quality (Chap-
ter 5). The questionnaire is distinct from the algorithmic BRS: sharing component
names does not establish equivalence between audience responses and computed
platform scores. Its proposed measurement model is

3.6
EST-P4: Participation and Evidence-Based Production
3.6.1
Statement
EST-P4 proposes that platform aordances shape opportunities for source appraisal,
correction, participation, and evidence-based media production. Reputation cues,
access to diverse sources, reection prompts, and contribution tools may support
these activities, but enabling a feature does not guarantee that a participant uses it
or produces a better contribution. The proposition concerns observable communi-
cation practices within a specied platform environment, not a hierarchy of learner
stages or a maximum on individual ability.
3.6.2
Operational Scope
The eld questionnaire measures audience evaluations, while the qualitative records
describe perceived opportunities and intentions. Neither establishes a causal im-
provement in task performance. The computational extension tests whether speci-
ed congurations change independently keyed claim-appraisal accuracy and sepa-
rately assessed production, holding the model, source library, initial network, and
budgets constant within paired runs.
The combined feedback-and-scheduling comparison addresses a conguration

CHAPTER 3. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK: EPISTEMIC SYSTEMS THEORY 50
bundle. Separate eects require the feature ablations specied in Section 5.10.1.
Contribution tools are held constant unless an additional task-specic intervention
explicitly varies them. A well-implemented comparison showing no meaningful per-
formance advantage, or worse performance, challenges the predicted benet in that
environment.
A permission check alone tests access control, not communication
quality.
Platform access ranks, audience ratings, task performance, and human
self-reported competence therefore remain distinct measurements.
3.7
Student Rating: Media Competence and Impact
The source code also uses the identier SR for a posterior over a broadcaster's la-
tent audience rating. That software variable is not the student competence con-
struct developed here. Throughout this thesis, Student Rating as competence names
the student-level outcome, whereas backend rating posterior names this separate
software quantity. Published NMLS evidence supports the choice of an external
competence instrument; it does not retroactively validate the backend variable.
Student Rating (SR) concerns the student's development as a critical media
consumer and responsible contributor. It is not the number of stars the student
gives a broadcast. Four objects must be kept distinct: SR concerns the student;
BRS concerns the broadcaster; PB concerns the listening experience; and stars pro-
vide a global evaluation of an episode. A learner can enjoy a broadcast without
developing competence, or develop competence while becoming more critical of the
broadcaster.
Thus a higher star response is neither a necessary nor a sucient
indicator of improved Student Rating.

CHAPTER 3. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK: EPISTEMIC SYSTEMS THEORY 51
3.7.1
A Published Media-Literacy Measure
The selected external instrument is the New Media Literacy Scale (NMLS; Koc &
Barut, 2016). Its development and cross-validation involved 1,226 university stu-
dents in Turkey and supported 35 items across four related factors.
It assesses
self-reported competence, not demonstrated task mastery. Its ve-point agreement
format and four-domain structure provide the human measurement basis for a possi-
ble later study. Agent answers to these items are secondary synthetic self-description
diagnostics, not validated student competence measurements. EST remains the the-
oretical framework.

CHAPTER 3. THEORETICAL FRAMEWORK: EPISTEMIC SYSTEMS THEORY 53
3.7.3
Meaning of Impact and Connection to EST
The next evaluation is computational: impact means a contrast in recorded agent
performance or exposure under assigned platform congurations, conditional on the
chosen models, anchors, tasks, and memory rules. It is not human learning merely
because the agent has a student persona. A later human impact claim would re-
quire its own assigned-condition comparison, pre-exposure competence measures,
and independent performance evidence. A delayed human assessment and an agent-
memory replay are dierent designs; neither is inferred from the other.
EST-P1 links specied platform features to opportunities and exposure; EST-
P2 concerns diversity and network constraints; EST-P3 concerns whether SR and
BRS support their intended interpretations; and EST-P4 concerns the student's
opportunities for more demanding participation and production. NMLS concerns
human self-reported media competence; agent responses in its format remain ex-
ploratory.
Platform access ranks, independently assessed task performance, and
questionnaire scores remain separate variables.

3.8
Scope Conditions and Potential Disconrmation
EST combines explanatory proposals with a normative requirement for measurement
accountability. These should not be tested in the same way. A poor instrument can
fail H3's validity requirement without disproving the desirability of EST-P3. Con-
versely, an association consistent with P1 does not establish the stronger proposition
that architecture dominates all user-level inuences.
Three scope conditions are essential.
First, an intervention must change
the feature named in the proposition, with exposure measured suciently to assess
implementation. Second, the outcome must represent the claimed construct: source
entropy is not factual accuracy, and PB is not a learning achievement measure.

EST should also accommodate interactions. The additive separation in Equa-

content interactions unless these are modelled explicitly. A future test must not
treat such interactions as zero merely because the schematic equation omits them.
